title: A transfer's alignment tail, filled with a literal pad
surface: gm_to_ub_pad(dst, src, n_burst=, burst_len_element=, src_stride_element=, dst_stride=, pad=) -- the pad keyword that finishes a burst's 32-byte alignment tail; CeilDiv / GetVecNum / GetVecIdx partitioning rows over participants
study_for: Where the pad actually lives. The backend prints `pad` into the `set_mov_pad_val` SPR before the transfer, which is where AscendC's own `DataCopyPadGm2UBImpl` puts it: mode state around the instruction, not an operand of it. Drop the keyword and the tail is not zeroed -- it keeps whatever the destination already held, which is the difference between a defined output and a plausible one.

Why the numbers are 9 and 16. Nine FP32 values are 36 bytes; the destination tile is 16 FP32, 64 bytes, two whole 32-byte blocks. The tail is the 28 bytes from 36 up to 64, and it exists because the transfer unit works in blocks while the burst length does not have to. A different dtype or a different burst moves that boundary, which is why the cases compare the whole tile rather than the copied part.

Why -1.5 and not 0. The value is 0xBFC00000, and `check_domain` refuses to run if the input carries it. That is what makes the comparison able to tell three states apart: a copied byte, a padded byte, and a byte nothing wrote -- the destination arrives NaN-poisoned, so the third one is visible too.

Only a literal pad is reachable. A run-time value raises `CceGap` at its source span: the SPR takes the value's bit pattern and the printer bitcasts it at compile time. The refusal is the API telling you where the boundary is, rather than the emitter inventing a store to get around it.
do_not_copy_when: You expect an unwritten tail to be zero. It is not, on any path here. Either you carry a pad value or you accept whatever the destination held, and the second one is only safe if you can name who wrote it last.

Your pad has to depend on the data. The instruction takes a compile-time bit pattern. A data-dependent fill is a separate vector store into the tail, with the event that orders it against the burst -- a different kernel, not a keyword change.

You are reusing the row partition without the row count. `CeilDiv(ROWS, GetVecNum())` with `ROWS = 4` divides four rows over the participants this launch has; on one participant that is all four. Copying the two lines into a kernel with a different row count, or more than one participant, changes which rows each core owns and the comparison here would not have caught it.
